title: Saks Global: When the Vendors Stop Shipping
deal_type: Chapter 11 (SDTX) following an out-of-court liability management exchange; DIP-to-equity plan with a liquidating sub-plan for Saks OFF 5TH

segments.name: situation
segments.direction: Warm and unhurried, two colleagues settling in; plain English, no jargon yet.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Welcome to Distressed Explainers. Today's story is Saks Global. It's the company that owns Saks Fifth Avenue, Neiman Marcus and Bergdorf Goodman, and in the space of eighteen months it went from a two point seven billion dollar acquisition to a Chapter 11 in Houston to being handed to its lenders. It's a great teaching case because almost every tool on a special situations desk shows up in it.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: So set it up for me. I know Saks as a store. I don't know Saks as a credit.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Start in December 2024. Hudson's Bay Company, the Canadian parent of Saks, closes the purchase of Neiman Marcus Group for about two point seven billion dollars. It puts the American businesses into a new holding company called Saks Global. The equity comes from Amazon, Salesforce, Authentic Brands and others. But most of the price is borrowed: two point two billion dollars of eleven percent secured notes due 2029, plus an asset-based revolver.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Eleven percent on two point two billion. That's about two hundred and forty million a year of interest just on the bonds.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Right, and hold that number, because the business was already struggling. By February 2025 the CEO wrote to suppliers admitting an eighteen-month backlog of unpaid bills. The fashion houses did the rational thing and stopped shipping. In the second half of 2025 the company received more than five hundred and fifty million dollars less inventory than it had planned for. Less inventory, less sales. Second quarter revenue fell thirteen percent to about one point six billion, and adjusted EBITDA was a loss of seventy-seven million.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: A loss. So the interest bill alone is larger than the earnings, and the earnings are negative.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Exactly. So in the summer of 2025 they did an out-of-court deal with the bondholders that raised six hundred million dollars of new money and split the bonds into three tiers. That bought five months. On December 31, 2025 they skipped a coupon of more than a hundred million dollars, and on January 13 and 14, 2026, Saks Global and a hundred and twelve affiliates filed Chapter 11 in the Southern District of Texas, in front of Judge Alfredo Pérez.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: And what happened in the case?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: The bondholder group that had funded the summer deal funded the bankruptcy too, with a two point six billion dollar loan. The company closed most of Saks OFF 5TH, a plan was confirmed on June 5, 2026, and on June 26 the company came out with a new name, Exemplar Luxury Group, forty-nine stores, about eight hundred and forty million dollars of debt instead of three point four billion, and owned by those lenders. The old equity, including Amazon's four hundred and seventy-five million, got nothing. Nothing is scheduled on the docket now, so today is about understanding how a desk read each step.

segments.name: concepts
segments.direction: Brisk and organized, like laying out a map on the table; each idea gets a clear one-paragraph intuition.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Let me name the six ideas this story turns on, then we'll take them one at a time. First, why companies get into distress. Moyer opens his book with the causes of financial distress, and Saks is a textbook stack of them: too much acquisition debt, an operating decline, and a working-capital spiral where your suppliers are your lenders.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Working capital as a cause of distress. I think of working capital as an accounting line, not a loan.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: For a retailer it is a loan. If you owe your vendors eighteen months of bills, they've financed you. When they stop, you have a liquidity crisis even if the balance sheet looked fine. Second idea: how a retailer's collateral is split. The asset-based lender, the ABL, gets first claim on inventory and receivables. The bonds get first claim on everything else. That split, and the ABL's covenants, decide how much cash the company can actually touch.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: So the bonds being secured doesn't mean they're secured by the stuff on the shelves.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Correct, and that surprises people. Third: the summer 2025 deal, which is called a liability management exercise. The company created a new subsidiary, sold new bonds out of it that rank ahead of everyone, and then let existing holders exchange into a ladder: first-out, second-out, third-out. Same eleven percent coupon, very different place in line. Moyer covers exchange offers as the out-of-court path. This is the modern, sharper-elbowed version.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: First-out, second-out, third-out. Those are payment positions, not lien positions?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Payment positions inside one lien. We'll unpack it. Fourth: DIP financing. Debtor-in-possession financing is the loan a company takes inside Chapter 11. Here it was two point six billion dollars, of which only one billion was new cash. The rest was existing bonds being rolled up into the loan. The DIP is where the fight for control of Saks was actually won.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Two point six billion with one billion new. Why would you structure it that way?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Because a rolled-up bond becomes a DIP claim, and DIP claims get paid first and get to convert into the company. Which brings us to the fifth idea, Moyer's fulcrum security. The fulcrum is the class where the value runs out: it's impaired, but it gets the equity. At Saks the fulcrum moved three times, from the original bonds, up to the new priority bonds, and finally to the DIP itself. The plan converted the DIP into ownership.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: And the sixth?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Structural subordination, meaning where the valuable asset sits in the corporate tree. The Saks flagship at 611 Fifth Avenue, appraised at around three point six billion dollars, is owned by an entity that never filed for bankruptcy. Amazon had rights at that level and fought the DIP over it. Value outside the debtor is one of the first things a desk maps. Let's take them in order.

segments.name: unfurl_causes_and_collateral
segments.direction: Teaching mode, patient; slow down on the numbers and let the guest restate them.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Start with the accounting a creditor cares about. Adjusted EBITDA was negative seventy-seven million dollars in the second quarter of fiscal 2025. When EBITDA is negative, leverage multiples are meaningless. What matters is cash interest versus liquidity. Across the three tiers of bonds there was about two point six billion at eleven percent, so roughly two hundred and ninety million a year of interest, and the coupon they skipped in December was more than a hundred million.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: And liquidity for a retailer means the ABL, right? How does that actually work?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: The ABL lends against a borrowing base: a percentage of eligible inventory and receivables. Availability is the borrowing base minus what you've drawn minus reserves. The ABL also has a covenant called minimum excess availability. At Saks that was two hundred million dollars, and it was raised to five hundred million as part of the restructuring. So when vendors stopped shipping, inventory fell, the borrowing base fell, and the cash the company could touch shrank exactly when it needed it most.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: That's the spiral. Fewer goods, less borrowing, less cash to pay vendors, fewer goods.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: That's the retailer death loop, and Moyer would classify it as a liquidity crisis that becomes a solvency crisis. Now the collateral split. At the petition date the ABL had about four hundred and forty-two million drawn. The second-out notes, for example, had a first lien on what the intercreditor calls Notes Priority Collateral, which is the brands, the equity of subsidiaries, owned property inside the debtors, and only a second lien on the ABL Priority Collateral, the inventory and receivables.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: So if I'm a bondholder and the company liquidates, the ABL takes the inventory proceeds first and I get what's left of that plus the rest.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Yes. And notice the size difference: four hundred and forty-two million of ABL against two point six billion of notes. The small lender holds the liquid collateral and controls the liquidity clock; the large lenders hold the story. A desk watches excess availability the way a doctor watches blood pressure. We could not source the actual borrowing base or the cash at filing, so on air I'll just say the filings we could read didn't break that out.

segments.name: unfurl_exchange
segments.direction: Engaged and slightly conspiratorial, walking through the mechanics of the deal step by step.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Now the summer deal. In May 2025 Saks hired Kirkland and Ellis and PJT Partners. On June 27 a new wholly owned subsidiary called SGUS sold three hundred million dollars of eleven percent senior secured asset-based notes to existing bondholders and lent the cash up to the operating company. On July 21 the company launched an exchange offer for the whole two point two billion of old notes.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Exchange into what?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Into a mix of three things. More of the SGUS notes, which everyone called the SPV notes, S P V for special purpose vehicle. Second-out notes issued by Saks Global. And third-out notes, also issued by Saks Global. All eleven percent, all due 2029. The difference is where you stand in line when the same collateral is sold.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Wait, what does first-out actually mean then, if it's not a separate lien?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Think of one lien, one pot of collateral, and an intercreditor agreement that says the pot pays tier one in full before tier two sees a dollar, and tier two in full before tier three. First-out, second-out, third-out. It's a payment waterfall, not a separate mortgage. The SPV notes were the first-out layer, and they got priority because they brought new money.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: And how did it settle?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: On August 8. SGUS issued four hundred and sixty-two and a half million of SPV notes, three hundred million for cash and a hundred and sixty-two and a half million in exchange. Saks Global issued one point four four billion of second-out notes and four hundred and forty-one million of third-out notes. About ninety-eight percent of the old notes tendered. Total new money, six hundred million. And because the exchange notes were issued at a discount, the company captured about a hundred and fifteen million dollars of debt reduction.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Ninety-eight percent tendered. Why so high? Nobody wanted to be left in the old bonds?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: That's the consent solicitation. Alongside the exchange the holders voted to amend the old indenture. We couldn't read the amendments themselves, but the structure tells you what they did: they permitted the SPV debt and the priority tiers. If you don't tender, you're left in a stripped bond that now sits behind everyone. That's the coercive element in a non-pro-rata exchange, and it's why the desk term for these is liability management exercise, or LME. Moyer teaches exchange offers as the cheaper alternative to Chapter 11; the twist since his edition is that they now reorder the creditors, not just extend them.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Non-pro-rata meaning different holders got different mixes?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Yes. Those who put in the six hundred million got the first-out paper. And the market's verdict came fast. By December the second-out notes were quoted around twelve cents on the dollar, down from about thirty earlier the same week. Twelve cents on a bond that is nominally first lien tells you the market thought value ran out inside the SPV layer. The exchange had bought five months, not a fix.

segments.name: unfurl_dip
segments.direction: Focused and precise, this is the heart of the episode; keep the numbers slow and the stakes clear.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: So we get to January 2026 and the DIP. Let's define it properly. A debtor-in-possession loan is post-petition financing that the court gives superpriority, meaning it's paid before every prepetition claim, and usually priming liens, meaning liens that jump ahead of existing secured lenders on the same collateral. Moyer covers this in his chapter on the Chapter 11 process. The DIP here was two point six billion dollars, made to SGUS, that same special purpose subsidiary.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Two point six billion into a company with negative EBITDA. Walk me through the pieces.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Three tranches. One: one billion dollars of new money, first-out, available in three draws, at Term SOFR plus eleven percent, paid in kind. Two: up to eight hundred and eight million of second-out DIP loans that replaced the SPV notes dollar for dollar, with no cash changing hands. That's a roll-up. Three: up to seven hundred and fifty-one million of third-out DIP loans that SGUS used to buy participations in second-out notes held by the DIP lenders.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Hang on. Paid in kind means the interest is added to principal rather than paid in cash?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Yes, PIK. The loan grows instead of draining cash. On top of that there were premiums: a six percent structuring premium, a two percent commitment premium, and an eight percent backstop premium for the parties who guaranteed to fund. All paid in kind. So on the billion of new money, the lenders started with roughly sixteen points of fees before a dollar of interest.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: And the roll-up. Why does it matter that the SPV notes became DIP loans?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Because a DIP claim is senior to everything and, in this plan, converts into the equity. So the roll-up moved eight hundred million of prepetition bonds to the front of the line. The third tranche is subtler: it gave the group's own second-out holdings a DIP-level claim through participations. A desk immediately asks whether second-out holders outside the group got the same offer, and Debtwire's read was that the plan would need amendments. We couldn't source the final treatment of the outside second-out holders, so I'll flag that as a gap.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Did the court just approve all of this?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: After a seven and a half hour first-day hearing on January 14. Amazon and a lender called Axonic objected. Their argument was about structure: the flagship at 611 Fifth Avenue is owned by a non-debtor under an entity called HoldCo II, Amazon had consent rights at that level, and it said the building already backed its nine hundred million dollar commercial agreement. Judge Pérez approved the interim DIP anyway, finding it was the only actionable financing and the alternative was liquidation. The company got five hundred and fifty million of liquidity that day, including four hundred million of new money. In February the final order went through with amendments, Amazon withdrew, and three hundred and thirty million went to vendors within two weeks.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: That's the structural subordination point. Amazon put in four hundred and seventy-five million of equity and still had to fight from outside the estate.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: And lost the equity entirely. The lesson is that where the asset sits in the tree, and who has consent rights at that box, matters more than the size of the cheque you wrote. There was also a one point five billion dollar ABL DIP with a creeping roll-up, where prepetition revolver borrowings are repaid with DIP borrowings over time, freeing about two hundred and forty million more.

segments.name: unfurl_fulcrum
segments.direction: Reflective, pulling the threads together; a little slower, giving the listener room to see the whole structure.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Now Moyer's central idea, the fulcrum security. Take the enterprise value, pay claims from the top down, and the class where the money runs out is the fulcrum. It's impaired, but it gets the reorganized equity, because everyone below it gets nothing and everyone above it gets paid. At Saks you can watch the fulcrum move.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Before the exchange it was the single class of old notes, presumably.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Yes. Press estimated by May 2025 that bondholders faced nearly a billion of losses on two point two billion, so equity was already out of the money. After the exchange, the twelve-cent quote on the second-out told you the fulcrum had moved up into the SPV notes. Then the DIP rolled the SPV notes into itself and added a billion of new money on top. So the DIP became the fulcrum, and the plan simply recognized it.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: What did the plan actually do?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: The company called it a dual-path plan. For the main debtors, a mechanism called the DIP Conversion: consenting DIP term loan lenders exchange their DIP claims for majority ownership of the reorganized company. The one billion of first-out new money was to be treated with take-back debt, meaning new debt issued to those same lenders, and the group also committed five hundred million of exit financing under a restructuring support agreement signed April 1. For Saks OFF 5TH there was a separate liquidating plan with a liquidation trust.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: And the unsecured creditors, the vendors?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: This is a nice Moyer point on how the plan treats unsecured claims. Two very different outcomes for the same legal class of creditor. Vendors the business couldn't reopen without, the fashion houses, were treated as critical vendors and paid in full: more than six hundred million dollars of prepetition claims over the case. Everyone else got a litigation trust funded with twenty million dollars, where the first twenty million of recoveries repays the company and the next eighty million is split between two beneficiary classes.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: So how would a desk have traded this?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Three positions. Own the new money: whoever wrote the six hundred million in 2025 and the billion in 2026 controlled the process and ended up with the company. Pentwater alone held about one point two billion of the group's paper, and Pentwater and Bracebridge each got two board seats. Second, trade claims: buying receivables from small vendors at a discount ahead of critical vendor approval is the classic trade, though we couldn't source whether it happened here. Third, avoid the third-out notes, which sat at the bottom of a secured stack that ran out of value. The debt went from three point four billion to about eight hundred and forty million: five hundred million of exit term loan, paid in kind for two years, and a three hundred and forty million ABL. We could not source the recovery percentages by class or the valuation in the disclosure statement.

segments.name: watch
segments.direction: Energetic wrap-up, practical and forward-looking; end on the reading list.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: So what to watch. The case is over, the plan went effective June 26, but the interesting questions are all post-emergence. One: the litigation trust. It preserves causes of action against pre-filing parties, and the twenty-million-then-eighty-million waterfall means the outcome is what unsecured creditors actually recover. Two: the OFF 5TH liquidation trust winding down the off-price business through its plan administrator.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: And the operating side? Same vendors, same negative EBITDA going in.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: That's three. The exit term loan pays interest in kind for two years, roughly fifty million a year, and the ABL costs about eighteen million this fiscal year. That's the runway. Four: Amazon, which threatened action in January and whose partnership was reported to be exited during the case. And five, anything on the flagship: it's a three point six billion dollar building in a non-debtor, and we could not source whether there's a mortgage on it.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: Give me the reading list. I now know the words.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Three documents, all on the Stretto case site for Saks Global Enterprises. First, the first-day declaration. It's the single best summary of the capital structure and the causes, and now you can read a sentence like 'first lien on Notes Priority Collateral and second lien on ABL Priority Collateral' and know what it means. Second, the DIP order and the DIP credit agreement: find the three tranches, the roll-up, and the premiums we discussed. Third, the disclosure statement, for the valuation, the liquidation analysis and the recovery table by class, which is the piece we couldn't source today.

turns.speaker: Guest
turns.text: And the August 2025 exchange press release for the tier structure.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Yes, and read it next to Moyer's chapter on out-of-court restructurings. You'll see exactly where the textbook ends and the modern LME begins. As always, this is education, not investment advice. Thanks for listening.
